episodes.213890: Initial shower and thunderstorm coverage during the morning hours of July 18, 2026 moved east of the region and allowed for ample recovery with respect to instability across the region during the late morning and early afternoon hours. The remnants of a MCS that tracked across Ohio and western Pennsylvania continued into northern Somerset County during the morning hours and produced multiple instances of tree damage as it continued into northern Bedford County in the early afternoon hours. At the same time, thunderstorm development across northwestern Pennsylvania began to rapidly show upscale growth within a strongly sheared and unstable environment, allowing for multiple instances of tree damage in Warren County. Storms began to quickly show signs of rotation as they moved further southeast into Elk County and produced wind damage, but no convergent patterns in damage were found. As these storms continues southeastward with continued rotation, a tornado occurred in northern Centre County and multiple instances of tree damage were observed in Clinton County. In the late afternoon hours, additional rotating cells came from western Pennsylvania, spawning an EF-2 tornado in Somerset County where widespread tree damage was observed. These cells also spawned three tornadoes, with an EF-1 in Clearfield County, an EF-2 in Huntingdon County, and an EF-0 in Blair County. Wind damage continues to be observed from these storms through the Lower Susquehanna Valley, mainly in the form of tree damage. Multiple rounds of storms in Clearfield and Somerset Counties also resulted in isolated instances of flash flooding on roadways.

episodes.214223: The overall synoptic pattern featured the subtropical high over the Central Rockies with easterly flow over most of the region. On the southern periphery of the subtropical high, an easterly wave traversed the region helping to increase the forcing for ascent and thus the potential for more widespread convective activity. A very moist airmass was present as PWAT values ranged between 1.8-2.2 across most of the lower elevations of central and southern AZ. The very moist airmass combined with MLCAPE values of around 500 J/KG was sufficient for the development of thunderstorms to produce heavy rainfall rates in excess of 1-2 per hour. With the flow aloft being on the weak side, with the steering motion at most 5 kts, the thunderstorm activity that developed was very slow moving, exacerbating the flood threat. During the evening hours on the 16th and continuing through the early morning hours on the 17th, a complex of thunderstorms developed just east of Phoenix, affecting much of the foothills and higher terrain areas before activity gradually clustered to the north of Phoenix metro and gradually weakening during the morning hours on the 17th. Another area of thunderstorms with heavy rainfall developed during the late morning/early afternoon hours across portions of southern Gila County, mainly between the Globe and San Carlos area. When all set and done, widespread amounts of 1-3 were observed with some areas along SR-88 between Tortilla Flat and Roosevelt Lake observing in excess of 4 based on rain gauge observations and doppler radar estimates, with much of the rainfall occurring within 1-3 hours. The heavy rainfall in this short time span lead to several flash flood incidents. In addition, during the afternoon hours on the 17th, an isolated nearly stationary severe storm developed east of Parker, AZ producing multiple inches of rain, causing the Bill Williams River to rise very rapidly and come within 0.50 feet of the gauge's historical peak, as well as a very large tree to be uprooted near the River Lodge Resort located south of the Parker Strip along the Lower Colorado River Valley.

episodes.215159: A tropical upper tropospheric trough (TUTT) across south Florida on July 16th shifted northwestward and closed off into an upper low over the northeastern Gulf on July 17th. The combination of deep tropical moisture and mid level cooler air overspread into northern Florida and Georgia supporting numerous showers and thunderstorms each afternoon and evening developing along the inland-moving sea breezes. A broad surface low then developed under the upper low in the northeastern Gulf and gradually deepened into Invest 91 on July 18th and then strengthened into Tropical Depression 2 on July 19th. Showers and thunderstorms rotated around the eastern side of the system shifting northward up the Florida peninsula July 19th into July 20th. A few strong to severe storms developed as the outer rainbands from TD 2 interacted with the sea breeze and outflow boundaries. On July 20th, mid-level drier air filtered into the area from the south triggering some stronger downbursts.

episodes.215718: A strong upper-level ridge moved over the northern Great Plains allowing a moist, tropical airmass to move over South-Central Texas. Precipitable water values increased to greater than 2.0 inches which were near or above the 95th percentile of climatological values for this part of July. Multiple rounds of excessive rainfall were triggered by mid-level disturbances around the southern periphery of the high and low-level outflow boundaries. This convection was aided by nocturnal low-level jet streaks which led to slow moving, back building thunderstorms. Most of South-Central Texas received more than two inches of rain. The greatest totals were over Uvalde and Kinney Counties where 20-30 inches occurred. Another local maximum of 15-20 inches was observed in central Kerr County. Ten to 15 inches were widespread from Del Rio to Hondo and northward to northeastern Edwards to western Gillespie Counties. Damage estimates were near $115 million across South-Central Texas.

episodes.216191: During the afternoon and evening hours on July 18th, scattered showers and thunderstorms developed across southern Indiana ahead of a cold front which was sinking toward the Ohio Valley. This allowed for around 2500 to 3000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE to develop during the peak heating hours, with forcing from the approaching cold front and a descending mid-level trough helping to develop thunderstorms across the region. Wind shear was seasonably strong thanks to the mid-level trough being relatively near the region, with around 20 to 25 knots of effective shear present to keep storms loosely organized. While most convection was sub-severe on this day, a couple particularly strong cells resulted in scattered wind damage across Dubois and Harrison County in southern Indiana.

episodes.216554: A cold front, trailing upper level low pressure, drove into West Virginia throughout the day on July 18th. The heavy downpours that accompanied the first round of activity in the morning set forth flash flooding across the northern half of the state, with creeks spilling out of their banks onto local roadways. episodes.217102: Another multiple day period of unsettled weather occurred between July 17th and 19th across the Ohio Valley. On July 17th, the synoptic pattern featured weak flow through much of the troposphere, with the region being on the eastern side of an expansive upper ridge. However, hot and humid conditions were present, allowing for between 2000 and 3000 J/kg of mixed-layer CAPE to develop across central Kentucky during the afternoon hours. Given the weak flow aloft, pulse convection was mainly experienced across the area, although a few stronger storm cores were able to produce downbursts resulting in isolated wind damage. Later in the evening, a cluster of storms across south central Kentucky congealed into a large mass of heavy rainfall, with precipitable water values exceeding 2 inches and decreasing instability allowing for efficient rainfall production. This resulted in isolated instances of flash flooding near Green River Lake. On the 18th, an approaching cold front and mid-level trough helped to increase the wind shear and forcing for storms, with more organized convection developing during the afternoon and evening hours. The strongest storm of the day went across the southwest side of the Louisville metro, producing several instances of wind damage. Finally, as the cold front sank to the south during the afternoon on July 19th, training thunderstorms in a rich moisture environment once again produced isolated flash flooding, this time in Cumberland and Clinton County.

This was the highest crest measured at that site since 1996.||A vehicle was swept by flooding into the Devils Draw near the confluence with Howard Draw north of Pandale on the evening of July 17, resulting in the death of one of the two occupants. The other was hospitalized with serious injuries. The Pecos River overtopped the Langtry Rd bridge at Pandale Crossing on the evening of July 17, contorting segments of the metal guardrails. A tornado touched down along Farnham road approximately 3 miles south-southwest of Sanford at 6:12 PM on July 18th. It caused sporadic EF-0 damage along Farnham road, mainly consisting of trees snapped or uprooted. There was minor damage to an old barn along the road and a gazebo was lifted into a pond. The tornado strengthened to EF-1 intensity (maximum winds of 95 mph) as it approached NY State Route 41, snapping and uprooting numerous trees, and power lines. The tornado crossed Oquaga Creek and caused more EF-1 level damage on Farnham Road and Old Plank Road. The damage mainly consisted of numerous downed trees, including a tree that fell onto a car. A home was damaged when the metal skirting was blown out from underneath it on Farnham Road. The tornado continued tracking southeast over a hill and paralleled Old Plank Road and Old Route 17 where it caused lighter sporadic tree damage at an EF-0 level. The weak tornado continued south and east, crossing State Route 17 just west of exit 83. It continued south and east, likely causing sporadic damage as it crossed over the inaccessible Whittacker Swamp State Forest. There was visible damage of numerous trees down and snapped along the hillside just west of River Road and State Highway 17. The weak tornado continued on, to the south and east causing light damage as it moved through the town of Hale Eddy, NY. Tornado briefly tracked into Wayne County PA with additional tree damage across the Delaware River along Penn York Road. The tornado crossed NY Route 17 again and moved across the town of Hancock, causing significant tree damage at the Hancock Golf Course. The tornado then crossed county highway 268 and the East Branch of the Delaware River. It restrengthened to EF-1 and caused significant tree damage mainly along the south bank of the river, along with some damage to out buildings and porches of residences. The tornado lifted just southeast of Peas Eddy Road as it moved up the hill.

A severe line of thunderstorms crossed into southwestern Sussex County near the Nanticoke River and Maryland border approximately 3 miles WSW of Bethel, impacting the Phillips Landing area with scattered tree damage. The storms continued in an ENE direction, passing across Broad Creek and surrounding rural areas, eventually reaching the Cypress Pointe neighborhood and adjacent homes and properties along Woodland Ferry Road. Several properties in this area sustained damage to trees, power lines, sheds, and fences consistent with wind gusts near 60 mph, but no structural damage was observed or reported in this immediate area.||The line of storms continued ENE from Woodland Ferry Road, reaching Oneals Road where a barn sustained loss of metal roof panels. This is where the peak estimated wind gusts of 75 mph was estimated to have occurred with these storms. There was tree damage observed in the vicinity of the barn as well. The storms continued ENE toward the area of Mount Zion Road between Seaford Road and US Route 13, where the last notable area of tree damage was observed. No significant wind damage from this portion of the line of storms was observed to have continued beyond this point.||Notable wind damage to trees reportedly occurred within the town of Seaford, but this was associated with a different segment of the severe line of thunderstorms which occurred between approximately 6:30 PM EDT and 6:35 PM EDT and was consistent with gusts near 60 mph.||There were no known injuries or fatalities from these storms.
